description: Concrete utility pole with a cheap flat LED flood panel strapped to it and aimed down the alley

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Tall precast concrete utility pole, square in section and tapering as it rises straight out of the ground with no base plate, a regular column of small round cast holes down its faces, one horizontal steel crossarm bolted across near the top carrying a row of squat barrel-shaped insulators standing upright on it, and strapped tight against the pole about two thirds of the way up a flat slab-shaped LED floodlight, a thin rectangular panel held in a U-shaped yoke bracket and tilted down and out to one side, its outward face one plain flat lens with a narrow frame around it Materials: Grey precast concrete with a coarse mottled surface, dark water staining and algae greening up the lowest two metres, rust bleeding from the cast holes and the strap clamp, chipped arrises exposing pale aggregate, grey painted floodlight body with a dusty grimy lens and a few dead insects on its upper edge, remains of torn paper flyers and staples across the lower shaft.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless pure WHITE studio matte. The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless white backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient. This is a studio cut-out, NOT an outdoor photograph: there must be no sky, no clouds, no buildings, no road and no overhead cables anywhere in the frame.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo. The lamp is switched OFF and emits no light.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 0.449 x 8.5 x 0.55 m. Cost: 656 triangles / 16000, 4 draw calls / 12, 4 materials / 8, 4 unique geometries / 16, 2 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 1.0, 0.986, 1.018], interior hole fractions [0.0003, 0.0, 0.0001, 0.0]).  Four components at 4 draw calls, 4 materials and 4 geometries against a hero2x ceiling of 12/8/16 -- 4% of the triangle ceiling, because the pole is 12 triangles as one frustum.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 0.449 x 8.500 x 0.550 m against the declared 0.45 x 8.5 x 0.55 -- exact on all three axes. Depth is the crossarm span; width is the pole plus the slab's far corner and nothing else, because this variant has no outreach arm. Proportion comes from the DECLARATION: silh.mjs puts the plate's subject at 285 x 919 px, implying 2.48 m of width at 8.5 m tall.

A tapered SQUARE frustum 0.225 m at the foot to 0.140 m at the top, chamfered cap, fourteen recessed cast holes down one face. The previous build was a bare smooth pipe with none of it. The shaft is 12 triangles as one frustum, which is why the crossarm, its insulators and the slab are all real geometry at 4% of the triangle ceiling.

A plain rectangular slab tilted 35 degrees nose-down with a bezel proud of its face and a recessed 18-band lens, carried on a steel band and a 75 mm stub with NO outreach arm. Both give-aways the asset notes lead with are now legible; the previous build had a tiny featureless box and no bracket, bezel or lens at all. The plate's panel stands slightly further off the pole than mine, which the declared 0.45 m width does not allow.

ONE crossarm spanning the declared 0.55 m depth with four cream porcelain pin insulators, each a skirt disc under a head disc. One arm and four insulators rather than the formal soi variant's two arms of six -- that difference is what the declared depth encodes, and the previous build had no arm and no insulators.

Four material layers: weathered concrete #9a998f, crossarm steel carrying its porcelain as a vertex colour, painted panel aluminium #8f979b and the lens. The housing is authored at luma 146 deliberately -- gatecrop's erased band is 55.5-60.5, a narrow window rather than a floor, and a face renders between about 0.55 and 1.0 of its albedo, so the safe range is luma < 55 or > 110. NOT carried: the plate's rust bleed from the crossarm bolts, which is directional where the tile is isotropic.

Green algae over the bottom 3.2 m as an axis tint multiplied into the concrete rather than a second material, with spalled patches as a post-construction tile on the same material. The plate's spalling is heavier and more clustered low down than the isotropic tile gives.

name: Clamp-On LED Soi Floodlight
nameTh: ไฟ LED ส่องซอยบนเสาไฟฟ้า
notes:
The second of two soi lighting variants and the informal one: a cheap flat LED flood panel clamped to a distribution pole with a steel band and pointed roughly down the alley, which is what most Bangkok back sois are actually lit by. The give-aways are that it hangs tight against the pole with no outreach arm at all -- hence the narrow 0.45 m width -- and that it is a plain rectangular slab rather than a shaped lantern. Deliberately shipped WITHOUT overhead cabling: a catenary of wires is thin geometry that costs draw calls, will not survive the reference reconstruction, and belongs to the level rather than to the prop. budgetClass pinned to hero against the hero2x its 8.5 m height would derive, because the prop is one tapered box, one crossarm and one flat panel, and these are placed down the whole length of every alley. Static: cast into the ground, so physics stays disabled.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED hero -> hero2x (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.
